cards.q: Why is an estimator being unbiased not enough to make it good?
pts: Unbiased only means E[θ̂] = θ — it says nothing about how spread out θ̂ is.
MSE = Var(θ̂) + Bias(θ̂)².
A slightly biased estimator (shrinkage, ridge, Ledoit–Wolf covariance) can have much lower MSE.
cards.pit: Also judge consistency, efficiency and robustness, not just bias.

cards.q: What is the central limit theorem in its basic i.i.d. form?
pts: X₁, …, Xₙ i.i.d. with mean μ and finite variance σ² > 0.
√n (X̄ₙ − μ) / σ converges in distribution to N(0, 1).
It describes the sample mean’s distribution, not the individual observations.
cards.pit: Infinite variance breaks this form; with fat tails the finite-sample approximation can be poor.

cards.q: What is the difference between bootstrap and cross-validation?
pts: Bootstrap: resample with replacement to approximate an estimator’s sampling distribution (standard errors, confidence intervals).
Cross-validation: split data into folds to estimate out-of-sample prediction error and tune hyperparameters.
Different goals: uncertainty of an estimate vs. generalization error of a model.
cards.pit: For time series use a block bootstrap and chronological / purged CV; i.i.d. resampling breaks the dependence.

pts: MLE: θ̂ = argmax p(data | θ).
MAP: θ̂ = argmax p(θ | data) = argmax p(data | θ) p(θ) — adds a prior.
Gaussian prior ⇒ MAP = L2 (ridge) penalty; Laplace prior ⇒ L1 (lasso) penalty.
As n → ∞ the likelihood dominates and MAP approaches MLE (under regularity).
cards.pit: MAP is not invariant to reparameterization, and neither estimator is unbiased in general.

cards.q: What is a p-value, and what is it not?
pts: The probability, assuming H₀ is true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.
It is NOT P(H₀ is true | data).
A small p-value is not a large effect: statistical significance ≠ economic significance.
cards.pit: Testing many strategies inflates false positives — adjust for multiple testing (e.g. Harvey–Liu–Zhu suggest t > 3).

cards.q: Why can heteroskedasticity cause problems in OLS inference?
pts: Under exogeneity, OLS coefficients stay unbiased and consistent.
But conventional standard errors are wrong ⇒ t-tests and confidence intervals are invalid, and OLS is no longer BLUE.
Fixes: White (HC) robust SEs; Newey–West (HAC) if errors are also autocorrelated; WLS/GLS for efficiency.
cards.pit: Robust standard errors fix inference only — not omitted-variable bias or endogeneity.

cards.q: What is the difference between confidence and prediction intervals?
pts: Confidence interval: for a parameter or the conditional mean E[y | x].
Prediction interval: for a new individual observation y — it adds the irreducible noise σ².
So the PI is wider; as n → ∞ the CI shrinks toward zero width but the PI does not.
cards.pit: Reporting a CI when someone asks about the next observation understates uncertainty.

pts: Expected squared prediction error = Bias² + Variance + irreducible noise σ².
More flexible models: bias goes down, variance goes up.
Regularization or ensembling trades a little bias for less variance ⇒ better out-of-sample error.
cards.pit: Training error keeps falling with complexity; only out-of-sample error shows the U-shape.
